uxorial.e: From Latin uxōrius (“of or pertaining to a wife; overly fond of one’s wife”) + English -al (suffix forming adjectives). Uxōrius is derived from uxor (“wife”) + -ius (suffix forming adjectives).

s.d: befitting or characteristic of a wife
Of or pertaining to a wife, or her genes or relatives.
x: Both are middle-class wives and mothers who are socially isolated and disenchanted with their marriages. [...] Unable to escape their uxorial and maternal roles, both retreat into themselves.

Jane [Eyre]'s nightmare of inarticulate desire suggests that more is at stake than common law, as Rochester seems to believe, or even ethical norms, such as she grapples with after learning his uxorial secret.
Riccabocca, the wiliest and most relentless of men in his maxims, melted into absolute uxorial imbecility at the sight of that mute distress.

uxoricide.e: Borrowed from French uxoricide or Latin uxor + English -icide.

s.d: a husband who murders his wife
the murder of a wife by her husband
(uncountable) The murdering of one's own wife.

uxorious.e: Borrowed from Latin uxōrius (“of or pertaining to a wife”), from uxor (“wife”) + -ious.

s.d: foolishly fond of or submissive to your wife
Very devoted and possibly submissive to one's wife; showing excessive uxorial devotion.
x: In truth, Richard was a fond—almost an uxorious husband.
Mr. Watkins Tottle was a rather uncommon compound of strong uxorious inclinations, and an unparalleled degree of anti-connubial timidity.
